en: Itivuttaka 112 Catukkanipāta Brāhmaṇadhammayāgavagga Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of offerings. What four? The offering of material things, the offering of Dhamma, the offering of fearlessness, and the offering of the supreme gift. (1) And what, bhikkhus, is the offering of material things? Here, someone offers food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps to recluses and brahmins. This is called the offering of material things. (2) And what is the offering of Dhamma? Here, someone teaches the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and which reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—to others. This is called the offering of Dhamma. (3) And what is the offering of fearlessness? Here, someone relieves the fear of those who are afraid, whether from lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, snakes, scorpions, or centipedes; or from human beings, non-human beings, fire, water, or kings; or from hostile kinsmen or rival clans. This is called the offering of fearlessness. (4) And what is the offering of the supreme gift? Here, someone establishes others in the noble eightfold path. This is called the offering of the supreme gift. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of offerings. When this was said, a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I am a giver of the four kinds of offerings. “What four, brahmin? “I give the offering of material things, the offering of Dhamma, the offering of fearlessness, and the offering of the supreme gift. “But how, brahmin, do you give these four kinds of offerings? “Master Gotama, I offer food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps to recluses and brahmins. Thus, Master Gotama, I give the offering of material things. I teach the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and which reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—to others. Thus, Master Gotama, I give the offering of Dhamma. I relieve the fear of those who are afraid, whether from lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, snakes, scorpions, or centipedes; or from human beings, non-human beings, fire, water, or kings; or from hostile kinsmen or rival clans. Thus, Master Gotama, I give the offering of fearlessness. I establish others in the noble eightfold path. Thus, Master Gotama, I give the offering of the supreme gift. “It is wonderful, brahmin! It is amazing, brahmin! How well you have spoken regarding these four kinds of offerings. But, brahmin, it is even more wonderful and amazing that you can speak thus after having learned it from whom? “From my father, Master Gotama. “And your father, brahmin? “From his father, Master Gotama. “And so on, brahmin? “Even seven generations back, Master Gotama. “It is wonderful, brahmin! It is amazing, brahmin! How well you have spoken regarding these four kinds of offerings, and how far back you can trace your lineage. But, brahmin, it is even more wonderful and amazing that you can speak thus after having learned it from the Teacher. “Who is that Teacher, Master Gotama? “That Teacher, brahmin, is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. “Is that so, Master Gotama? “Yes, brahmin. “If that is so, Master Gotama, we go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”
The Discourse on the World.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Bhikkhus, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata."
The Tathāgata is detached from the world.
Monks, the origin of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata;
the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata.
“Bhikkhus, the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata;
the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata.
The practice leading to the cessation of the world, bhikkhus, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.”
The practice leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata.

Monks, whatever in this generation—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated by the mind: [all that has been fully understood by the Tathāgata].
Because that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata with the mind,
he is therefore called the "Tathāgata. And,
monks, on whatever night the Tathāgata awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and on [whatever night]...
In the night, he attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue;
whatever he speaks, utters, or explains during that interval, all that is exactly so and not otherwise.
Therefore, he is called the “Tathāgata.”
Monks, the Tathāgata acts as he speaks, and speaks as he acts;
because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts,
he is therefore called the “Tathāgata.”

“Bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power;
therefore he is called ‘Tathāgata.
Thus the Blessed One spoke on this matter.
In this regard, it is said:
“Having directly known the entire world,
and the world exactly as it is;”
Detached from the entire world,
unattached to the entire world—
he is indeed the wise one who has overcome all.
The liberator from all bonds has touched the supreme peace,
Nibbāna, which is free from fear from every side.
He is the Buddha whose taints are exhausted,
free from distress, with all doubts severed,
having attained the destruction of all kamma.
Liberated through the destruction of the substrata.
He is that Blessed One, the Buddha;
he is the unsurpassed lion.
He set in motion the Wheel of Brahma for the world with its gods;
thus, both gods and humans—
Those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha gather together and pay homage to him,
the Great One, free from timidity.
The tamed is best among those being tamed;
the peaceful sage is best among those practicing peace;
the liberated is foremost among those seeking liberation.
The best among those who ferry others across has himself crossed over.
Thus they pay homage to him,
the great one who is free from timidity.
"In the world with its devas, there is no person who is your equal.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The Thirteenth [Chapter].
The Section of Fours is finished.
Its summary verse:
The Brahmin Sulabha knows [this];
craving is the ascetic virtue of Brahmā;
the deceitful men are of great service.
"Accomplished with the world," thus [ends] the Thirteen.
This is the compendium of suttas from the Twenty-Seven Section.
The Dukkaṃ [chapter] comprises twenty-two suttas;
likewise, there are thirty-five on the *atthaka* [group], and thirteen on the *catukka* [group]. Such is this [section].
In the past, for the sake of long endurance,
the Arahants recited and established one hundred and twelve suttas.
They call that by the name *Itivuttaka*.
The *Itivuttaka* Pāḷi is finished.
